column1: What distinguishes a real-world problem from an assessment problem?
column2: It has not been framed for you, and it is not guaranteed to have a solution.

column1: In the T-shaped model, what does the vertical stroke represent?
column2: Depth of knowledge in at least one discipline.

column1: In the T-shaped model, what does the horizontal stroke represent?
column2: Breadth about innovation that lets you work effectively with professionals of other disciplines to bring ideas to life.

column1: Is a person with broad knowledge but no deep discipline T-shaped?
column2: No. The vertical stroke is mandatory; breadth alone is a dash, not a T.

column1: Who is quoted arguing that teaching engineering fundamentals is "not enough"?
column2: Richard Miller, US National Academy of Engineering.

column1: According to Richard Miller, what will doubling down on more hard sciences and maths achieve?
column2: It will not help. Grand Challenges need engineering expertise but won't be solved by engineers alone.

column1: What two things does Miller say engineering education must add?
column2: Both a skillset and a mindset.

column1: Which accord makes T-shape skills part of professional engineer sign-off in New Zealand?
column2: The Washington Accord, via Engineering New Zealand.

column1: Who developed the fixed/growth mindset framework?
column2: Carol Dweck.

column1: Define a fixed mindset.
column2: The belief that your abilities are innate and unchangeable.

column1: Define a growth mindset.
column2: The belief that ability is something you can improve through practice.

column1: Are fixed and growth mindsets two categories of person?
column2: No. They exist on a continuum, and you sit at different points for different skills.

column1: Under a fixed mindset, how is failure viewed?
column2: As permanent.

column1: Under a growth mindset, how is failure viewed?
column2: As a chance to learn and even to pivot.

column1: Under a fixed mindset, how is critical feedback received?
column2: As a personal attack.

column1: Under a growth mindset, how is critical feedback received?
column2: As a chance to improve and develop new systems.

column1: How does mindset affect task choice?
column2: Fixed chooses easier tasks with minimal effort; growth embraces challenging tasks and works hard to improve.

column1: How does mindset affect response to obstacles?
column2: Fixed is likely to give up; growth treats obstacles as a chance to experiment and problem-solve.

column1: What is the focus under a fixed vs growth mindset?
column2: Fixed focuses on measurable accomplishments; growth focuses on a journey of continual improvement.

column1: How does mindset affect creative risk-taking?
column2: Fixed is less likely to take creative risks; growth treats them as a way to innovate and improve.

column1: Why is the fixed mindset internally consistent?
column2: If talent is fixed, effort is pointless: "why bother improving? Why even try?"

column1: What is the biological basis offered for growth mindset?
column2: Neuroplasticity: learning new things builds new neural pathways, especially as you get older.

column1: What everyday example of neuroplasticity was given?
column2: Slow recovery after a stroke, though the same process runs in healthy brains all the time.

column1: What example was given of a real limit on growth mindset?
column2: Buying figure skates at 14 and never becoming a figure skater, because of a physical ceiling.

column1: Define grit.
column2: Passion and perseverance for your goals, over a sustained period of time.

column1: Which clause separates grit from ordinary motivation?
column2: Over a sustained period of time.

column1: Who is grit associated with?
column2: Angela Duckworth, author of the book Grit.

column1: Name grit's four pillars.
column2: Passion/interest, deliberate practice, sense of purpose, sense of hope.

column1: What does the passion/interest pillar do?
column2: It makes determination possible: it is very hard to be determined about something you are not interested in.

column1: What does the deliberate practice pillar do?
column2: It covers the fact you won't manage it first time; it supplies patience, resilience and determination to keep going.

column1: What does the sense-of-purpose pillar do?
column2: It carries you through days you don't enjoy, by connecting them to a greater goal.

column1: What does the sense-of-hope pillar do?
column2: It sustains you when the goal looks unachievable, so you may overcome and achieve it anyway.

column1: What is the claimed relationship between talent and grit?
column2: They are unrelated, and possibly inversely related.

column1: What mechanism is proposed for talent reducing grit?
column2: Talented people have always found things easy, so they never learned to fail or built perseverance tools.

column1: Is grit fixed?
column2: No. It is described as something you can really work on.

column1: Where in Systems Week does the hope pillar get tested?
column2: Around Wednesday afternoon, when initial excitement gives way to despair.

column1: What does the marshmallow test measure?
column2: Impulse control, and willingness to strive for a bigger goal by delaying instant gratification.

column1: What is the caveat given about the marshmallow test?
column2: It also predicts people who simply don't like marshmallows; all tests have flaws.

column1: Why is failure argued to be professionally useful?
column2: Thinking about why and when you fail identifies specific weak spots you can then target.

column1: What three-step sequence turns failure into improvement?
column2: Failure, then diagnosis of the specific gap, then targeted effort on that gap.

column1: Why is failing earlier better than failing later?
column2: People who first fail at 45-55 find it much harder than those who set ambitious goals, failed earlier, and bounced back.

column1: What happens when a task is too easy?
column2: You complete it and learn nothing.

column1: What happens when a task is too hard?
column2: You can't do it, so you also learn nothing.

column1: Where does learning actually occur?
column2: In the discomfort zone: just hard enough, but not too hard.

column1: Is discomfort a cost of learning or a signal?
column2: A signal that you are in the band where growth happens.

column1: What does SMART stand for?
column2: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

column1: What letter does the lecturer propose adding to SMART, and why?
column2: H for Hard, to push you toward stretchy, ambitious goals.

column1: Which two elements of SMART-H pull against each other?
column2: Achievable and Hard.

column1: State the principle "coherence beats cleverness".
column2: A solution gains credibility only when all its parts tell the same story; otherwise decision-makers fixate on inconsistencies.

column1: Which four artefacts must tell the same story?
column2: The strategic case, options analysis, CBA metrics, and rollout plan.

column1: What is the stated corollary to "coherence beats cleverness"?
column2: Evidence is a team sport.

column1: Why isn't communication style a soft extra?
column2: It is an input to the overall system's success; a poor style can create a negative feedback loop.

column1: Who is the T-shaped people quote attributed to?
column2: Prof. Tina Seelig, Executive Director of the Stanford Technology Ventures Program.

column1: What label does the slide put on the T's horizontal bar?
column2: Innovation & Collaboration.

column1: What label does the slide put on the T's vertical stem?
column2: Discipline Knowledge.

column1: State Duckworth's first equation.
column2: Effort x Talent = Skill.

column1: State Duckworth's second equation.
column2: Skill x Effort = Achievement.

column1: What is the significance of effort appearing in both Duckworth equations?
column2: Effort counts twice: it builds the skill and converts that skill into achievement. Talent appears only once.

column1: What reflective question is attached to the Interest pillar?
column2: What question will compel you to stay gritty?

column1: What reflective question is attached to the Purpose pillar?
column2: How can you connect what you do to the well-being of others?

column1: Whose quote anchors the Interest pillar?
column2: Jeff Bezos - if you're not passionate about what you're working on, you won't be able to stick with it.

column1: What question did Duckworth use to stay interested through graduate school?
column2: What makes people successful and why?

column1: Does interest require enjoying every part of the work?
column2: No. Gritty people have chores they don't enjoy, but are captivated by the endeavour as a whole.

column1: What does deliberate practice target, per the Practice pillar?
column2: Your weaknesses, over and over, for hours a day, week after month after year.

column1: What is the stated enemy of grit in the Practice pillar?
column2: Complacency - to be gritty is to resist complacency.

column1: How many people did Duckworth survey for the purpose finding?
column2: Over 16,000 adult Americans.

column1: What correlates with higher scores on the Grit Scale?
column2: Higher scores on purpose - grittier people seek a meaningful, other-centered life.

column1: What kind of hope does grit depend on?
column2: The expectation that our own efforts can improve our future - agency, not general optimism.

column1: What belief does the hope pillar require?
column2: An enduring belief that your skills are malleable and not set in stone.

column1: What exercise is suggested to build the hope pillar?
column2: Recall a time you learned something you thought you never could - driving a car, a new sport, a new software program.

column1: What newspaper headline appears alongside the grit panels?
column2: Do You Keep a Failure Resume? Here's Why You Should Start - failure isn't a roadblock, it's part of the process.

column1: Give three fixed-mindset statements from the slide.
column2: I'm either good at it or I'm not; my potential is predetermined; when I'm frustrated, I give up.

column1: Give three growth-mindset statements from the slide.
column2: Failure is an opportunity to grow; challenges help me to grow; feedback is constructive.

column1: How does each mindset complete the sentence 'Failure is...'?
column2: Growth: an opportunity to grow. Fixed: the limit of my abilities.

column1: What shape is used to depict the ENGGEN 403 course structure?
column2: A honeycomb of twelve hexagonal components.

column1: Which two honeycomb cells are the assessments?
column2: Team Project (the dress rehearsal) and Systems Week.

column1: Which honeycomb cell is not taught in the course?
column2: Technical Know-How - it comes from your degree and experiences.

column1: What does the honeycomb encode by making Technical Know-How the same size as every other tile?
column2: That your discipline is one capability of twelve, not the foundation the others rest on - the T-shape claim drawn.

column1: When does Systems Thinking appear in the course?
column2: Weeks one and three.

column1: In which week is the Team Project, and what is it called?
column2: Week 6, described as the dress rehearsal.

column1: What is the McKinsey Workshop for?
column2: Learning how the pros handle high-pressure projects, in week 7.

column1: On the closing graph, what are the axes?
column2: Success on the y-axis, your career on the x-axis.

column1: On the closing graph, does the fixed-mindset line go up?
column2: Yes - it still rises, just shallowly. Nobody is being told they will fail.

column1: What is the key feature of the closing success graph?
column2: The grit/growth line branches off the fixed line partway along, and the course is positioned at that branch point.
